Priority system

items: ★★★ Very high priority — memorize the definition, example, and at least one related distinction.
★★ High priority — understand the concept and be able to explain it briefly.
★ Extension — recognize the term and know its basic meaning.

blocks.x: Master coverage: 419 unique key terms.
Recommended study order

items: Memorize the ★★★ terms in Applied Linguistics, SLA, teaching methods, assessment, and linguistics first.
Study the major distinctions. These are particularly useful for multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
Practice explaining each important term in one or two sentences without looking at the definition.
For essay writing, use terminology naturally and accurately rather than forcing many technical words into one paragraph.
When you meet a new term, connect it to an example from an English classroom. This makes the definition easier to remember.
After mastering the ★★★ terms, move to ★★ terms and then the extension terms.

head: Distinction
Exam Shortcut
rows: Linguistics studies language systematically; Applied Linguistics applies language knowledge to real-world language problems, especially teaching and learning.
Semantics concerns meaning encoded in language; pragmatics concerns meaning interpreted in context.
Cohesion is the linguistic linking of text; coherence is the overall logical and meaningful connection of ideas.
Approach = beliefs; Method = organized teaching plan; Technique = specific classroom procedure.
Acquisition emphasizes natural development through meaningful exposure/use; learning emphasizes conscious study or knowledge.
Competence is underlying knowledge; performance is actual language use.
Synonymy concerns similar meanings; hyponymy concerns a category/member relationship.
Homonymy involves identical forms with unrelated meanings; polysemy involves multiple related meanings.
Phonetics studies physical speech sounds; phonology studies how sounds function in a language system.
A phoneme is a smallest contrastive sound unit; a morpheme is a smallest meaningful or grammatical unit.
Descriptive grammar describes actual use; prescriptive grammar states preferred or standard rules.
Form is the grammatical shape; function is the communicative purpose.
Input is language received; output is language produced.
Positive transfer helps learning; negative transfer contributes to errors.
Direct speech acts match grammatical form and function; indirect speech acts do not.
Positive face is the desire for approval; negative face is the desire for freedom from imposition.
Equality gives the same treatment/opportunity; equity provides fair support according to different needs.
Assessment gathers evidence about learning/performance; evaluation makes judgments about quality, value, or effectiveness.

terms.d: A relationship between linguistic choices that can substitute for one another in the same position.

terms.d: A relationship between the meanings or forms of words.

terms.d: Creative or humorous use of language based on meanings, sounds, or forms of words.

terms.d: The process through which learners acquire word forms and grammatical markers.

terms.e: Students explain the story to a partner.

terms.d: The study of how people develop knowledge and ability in a language learned after their first language.

sections.title: Overview: how the theories fit together

blocks.x: Education theories are tools for thinking, not recipes. Each answers a different question: how people learn, how to set goals and sequence a lesson, how to motivate and manage a class, and why we teach at all. Good teachers combine them. One lesson might use Bloom's levels to write the objectives, Gagné's events to sequence the stages, Vygotsky's scaffolding during practice, and formative feedback to decide what to teach next.

blocks.x: Theories are not competing “right answers”. Evidence is stronger for some ideas than for others. For example, retrieval practice and formative feedback are well supported, while matching teaching to a learner's “learning style” is not. Where an important criticism exists, the section says so.

Behaviorism explains learning as a change in observable behavior produced by the environment. It dominated psychology and teaching from the early 1900s to the 1950s. It is the basis of drills, rewards and many classroom-management systems.
Branches and key figures

head: Branch
Key figures
Core idea
Classroom link
rows: A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers a conditioned response. Related ideas: extinction, generalization, discrimination.
Emotional associations: a safe, positive classroom builds positive feelings toward a subject; test anxiety can be a conditioned response.
Learning is forming stimulus–response connections. Law of Effect (satisfying results strengthen a response), Law of Exercise, Law of Readiness.
Practice with feedback; reward correct responses.
Behavior is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement increases behavior, punishment decreases it.
Praise, token systems, shaping a skill step by step, programmed instruction.

blocks.x: Operant conditioning: four kinds of consequence

head: Consequence
What happens
Effect on behavior
Example
rows: Praise or a sticker for a complete answer
A learner who has been working well is excused from a boring task
Losing a few minutes of free time

blocks.x: Schedules of reinforcement

items: Continuous: every correct response is reinforced. Fastest learning, but the behavior fades quickly when reinforcement stops.
Fixed-ratio: reinforcement after a set number of responses.
Variable-ratio: after an unpredictable number of responses. Produces steady behavior that is hardest to extinguish.
Fixed-interval: after a set amount of time.
Variable-interval: after unpredictable amounts of time.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Give specific, immediate feedback (“Good use of the past tense in sentence 2”) instead of general praise.
Break a skill into small steps and reinforce each step (shaping).
Use short repeated drills for skills that must become automatic: multiplication facts, spelling, pronunciation patterns, vocabulary.
Set a few clear rules with consistent consequences. If you use points or tokens, plan how to fade them out.
In English teaching, behaviorism underlies the Audiolingual Method: pattern drills with stimulus, response and reinforcement.

blocks.x: Maths: the class practises the 7× table in short daily drills with quick feedback. Each learner colours a progress chart, and the class earns a short game when everyone improves.

Behaviorism ignores thinking, understanding and motivation. Heavy use of external rewards can reduce interest in tasks learners already enjoy (the overjustification effect). Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that behaviorism cannot explain creative language use.
Reinforcement is not punishment. Negative reinforcement increases behavior by removing something unpleasant; punishment decreases behavior.

Cognitivism (from the 1950s, the “cognitive revolution”) studies the mental processes between stimulus and response: attention, perception, memory, thinking and problem-solving. Learning is seen as receiving, organizing and storing information so that it can be retrieved and used.
The information-processing model (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968)

items: Sensory memory holds raw input for a very short time (from a fraction of a second to a few seconds). Attention decides what moves on.

Working (short-term) memory holds and manipulates a small amount of information for seconds to about a minute. Capacity is limited: Miller (1956) suggested “7 ± 2” items; later estimates are nearer 4 chunks.
Long-term memory is a large, lasting store organized into schemas. Information gets there through meaningful encoding, connection to what is known, and repeated use.
Retrieval brings information back. Each successful retrieval strengthens the memory.

blocks.x: Branches and key theories

head: Theory
Key figure
Core idea
Classroom link
rows: Working memory has a central executive, a phonological loop (sound) and a visuospatial sketchpad (images); an episodic buffer was added in 2000.
Combine words with pictures; avoid asking learners to read one text while listening to another.
Deep, meaning-based processing produces stronger memory than shallow processing of sound or appearance.
Ask “why” and “how”; have learners explain, compare and apply.
Knowledge is organized in schemas. New information is understood by connecting it to existing schemas.
Activate prior knowledge; use concept maps and graphic organizers.
Learning is meaningful when new ideas are linked to existing knowledge. Advance organizers prepare the learner.
Begin with an overview, a key question or a short introductory text before the details.
Verbal and visual information are processed in separate channels; using both improves memory.
Pair explanations with diagrams, photos or gestures.
Working memory is limited. Intrinsic load comes from the difficulty of the content, extraneous load from poor presentation, and germane load from the effort of building schemas.
Cut extraneous load; use worked examples, chunk content, and fade support as skill grows.
People learn better from words and pictures together than from words alone, following principles such as coherence, signaling, spatial contiguity and segmenting.
Keep slides clean; put labels next to the parts they describe.

blocks.x: Evidence-based study strategies

items: Retrieval practice: recalling information without notes, for example a low-stakes quiz, strengthens memory more than rereading.
Spaced practice: spreading study over time beats cramming (Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, 1885).
Interleaving: mixing different problem types improves the ability to choose the right method.
Elaboration and concrete examples: explain ideas in your own words and attach examples.
Dual coding: combine words and visuals.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Open with a 3-to-5-question retrieval quiz on the previous lesson.
Chunk content into small steps and check understanding after each chunk.
Show a worked example before independent problems, then gradually remove the steps.
Use organizers, mnemonics and clear structure so learners can build schemas.
Remove decoration that does not help learning.

blocks.x: English reading lesson: begin with a picture and three prediction questions (activating schema). Pre-teach five key words with pictures (dual coding). Read in two short chunks with a question after each. Finish with a no-notes recall quiz.
The models simplify (the brain is not literally a computer), and cognitivism pays less attention to emotion, culture and social context.
Working memory is limited; long-term memory is practically unlimited. Know the three kinds of cognitive load: intrinsic, extraneous, germane.

Constructivism holds that learners actively build knowledge by connecting new experiences to what they already know, rather than receiving it ready-made. Its branches differ mainly on whether construction is individual (Piaget) or social (Vygotsky).

Cognitive conflict, hands-on exploration, tasks matched to the learner's stage.
Learning happens first between people and then inside the learner (internalization). Language and culture are tools of thought.
Group work, dialogue, scaffolding, peer teaching.
Learners discover principles with guidance. Key ideas are revisited at increasing depth. Scaffolding was described by Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976).
Guided discovery; revisit topics each term with more complexity.
Learning by doing and reflecting on experience; school should connect to real life.
Learning is participation in a community of practice, moving from legitimate peripheral participation to full membership.
Knowledge is constructed by the individual and does not copy an independent reality; it is judged by whether it works.
Value learners' own interpretations; ask for explanations.

blocks.x: Piaget's key processes: assimilation (fitting new information into an existing schema), accommodation (changing the schema to fit new information), and equilibration (balancing the two). Ages are approximate, and later research shows children can do more than Piaget estimated.
Key Vygotsky ideas

items: Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help.
More Knowledgeable Other (MKO): anyone or anything with more skill: teacher, peer, parent, software.
Scaffolding: temporary, adjustable support that is gradually withdrawn as the learner becomes capable.
Private speech: children talk aloud to guide their own thinking; it later becomes inner speech.
Language is the main tool of thought.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Start from learners' ideas: ask what they already think (a KWL chart works well).
Use tasks built around a problem or question, then discuss the reasoning.
Form mixed-ability groups with clear roles so that peers explain to each other.
Scaffold in steps: model, prompt, give a sentence frame or checklist, then remove it.
Ask for explanations: “How do you know?”, “Why does that work?”

blocks.x: Science: groups predict which objects float, test them, then explain the pattern. A sentence frame (“I predict that … because …”) supports weaker writers. Moral and Civics: groups discuss a real school problem and agree a set of class rules.
Constructivist teaching needs time and strong teacher guidance. Minimal-guidance discovery works poorly for novices (Kirschner, Sweller and Clark, 2006). Piaget's stages are criticized as too rigid.
Piaget: assimilation versus accommodation. Vygotsky: ZPD, MKO, scaffolding. “Social constructivism” is usually linked to Vygotsky.

Albert Bandura's social cognitive theory (earlier called social learning theory) says people learn by observing others, and that thoughts, beliefs and the environment all influence behavior. It bridges behaviorism and cognitivism.
Four processes of observational learning

items: Attention: the learner notices the model. Models who are competent, respected or similar to the learner get more attention.
Retention: the learner remembers what was seen, as images or words.
Reproduction: the learner is able to perform the behavior, and improves with practice and feedback.
Motivation: the learner expects a reward or sees others rewarded (vicarious reinforcement).

Seeing a model rewarded or punished changes the observer's behavior.

Belief in one's ability to succeed at a task. Sources: mastery experiences (strongest), vicarious experiences, social persuasion, and physiological and emotional states.
Give achievable challenges, show success of similar peers, offer honest encouragement, reduce anxiety.
The person (beliefs), the behavior and the environment influence each other.
Work on the climate, the task and the learner's beliefs together.
Learners set goals, monitor and evaluate their own behavior.

In the classroom

items: Model the process, not only the answer: think aloud as you solve a problem or write a sentence.
Use peer models, and point out role models of effort as well as of achievement.
Choose tasks that are slightly challenging so success builds self-efficacy.
Teach and model positive self-talk (“I can try another way”).
Remember that learners copy what teachers do as well as what teachers say.

blocks.x: English speaking: the teacher models a short dialogue with a confident learner, then pairs perform it. A nervous learner succeeds, which also raises the belief of similar learners that they can do it.
Observational learning can occur without direct reinforcement. Learning is not the same as performance: a learner may learn something and not show it until motivated.

sections.title: Humanism and adult learning (Maslow, Rogers, Knowles)

blocks.x: Humanistic education focuses on the whole person: feelings, needs, values, choice and personal growth. The teacher is a facilitator who creates a safe, respectful climate. It influenced student-centered teaching and adult education.
Key theorists

head: Theorist
Key ideas
Classroom link
rows: Hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualization. Lower (deficiency) needs must be reasonably met before higher (growth) needs motivate.
Check basic needs such as hunger, rest and safety; build belonging and respect before demanding high performance. The order is not rigid.

Person-centered learning (Freedom to Learn, 1969). The teacher is a facilitator who shows empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard. Significant learning is self-initiated and personally relevant.
Learner choice, listening, personal relevance, respectful feedback.

Andragogy (adult learning). Adults need to know why they are learning, are self-directing, bring experience, are ready to learn what they need, are problem-centered and are motivated mainly from within.
In teacher training and adult classes: real problems, sharing of experience, choice.
Self-determination theory: autonomy, competence and relatedness are basic psychological needs (see Motivation theories).
Offer choices, achievable challenge and a cooperative climate.
Heutagogy: self-determined learning, where the learner decides what and how to learn.

items: Physiological: food, water, rest, so allow breaks and notice hunger or tiredness.
Safety: physical and emotional safety, so use clear routines and a firm approach to bullying.
Love and belonging: a class community where nobody is excluded.
Esteem: recognition of effort and achievement; real responsibilities.
Self-actualization: creativity, projects and personal goals.

items: Learn and use learners' names; build relationships first.
Make rules together so learners feel ownership.
Offer choices of topic, task or product.
Give feedback on the work, not on the person.
Invite learners' opinions and feelings; use learning journals.

Humanistic claims are hard to test, and Maslow's order is not universal. “Student-centered” does not mean the teacher does nothing: structure and clear goals still matter.
Maslow: hierarchy of needs. Rogers: facilitator, person-centered learning. Knowles: andragogy.

Null (Elliot Eisner): what is left out and not taught.
Orientations: subject-centered, learner-centered, problem-centered; integrated (interdisciplinary).

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Plan backward: outcome first, then evidence, then activities.
Check alignment: objective, activity and assessment should match.
Use needs analysis to decide what learners need before choosing content.
Revisit key ideas across units with increasing depth (spiral).

blocks.x: Backward design for a Grade 8 geography unit on rivers. Big idea: people and rivers affect each other. Evidence: groups present a river-management proposal. Activities: map rivers, study a case, debate uses of water.
Tyler: four questions, product model. Taba: teacher-driven, inductive. UbD: begin with the end. ADDIE: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation.

sections.title: Motivation theories (SDT, expectancy-value, attribution, L2 motivation)

blocks.x: Motivation explains why learners start, continue or stop learning. It can be strengthened by the way teachers design tasks, give feedback and build relationships.
Major theories

head: Theory
Key figure(s)
Core idea
Classroom application
rows: Doing something for its own interest versus for a reward or to avoid a penalty.
Make tasks interesting and meaningful; use rewards sparingly.

Three basic needs support internalized motivation: autonomy, competence, relatedness. Regulation runs from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated to intrinsic motivation.
Offer choices (autonomy), achievable challenge and feedback (competence), a cooperative class (relatedness).
Effort depends on expecting to succeed and valuing the task (interest, importance, usefulness, cost).
Raise success expectations; explain why the task matters.
People explain success and failure by causes (ability, effort, task difficulty, luck) that differ in locus, stability and controllability.
Help learners link results to effort and strategy, which they can control.
Belief in one's own capability to succeed.
Mastery experiences and models (see Social cognitive theory).
Mastery goals (learn and improve) versus performance goals (look capable or beat others).
Stress progress and improvement; avoid public ranking.
A growth mindset (abilities can develop) versus a fixed mindset.
Praise strategy, effort and progress; treat mistakes as information. Effects of mindset programs are modest and depend on how they are taught.
Second-language learners may want to join the target community (integrative) or gain a practical benefit such as a job (instrumental).
Connect English to both interests in the culture and career goals.
Ideal L2 self (the user I want to become), ought-to L2 self (duties and others' expectations), and L2 learning experience (the classroom).
Ask learners to picture themselves using English in the future; make lessons a positive experience.
Design each lesson to include all four.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Open with a hook that connects to learners' lives (relevance).
Offer choices of topic, task or product.
Set short-term goals and show progress, for example with a checklist or chart.
Give feedback on effort and strategy: “Using a table to organize the data made your answer clear.”
Make tasks challenging but achievable, because success builds confidence.

blocks.x: Rewards can undermine interest if they feel controlling or are given for tasks learners already enjoy (the overjustification effect).
SDT has three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness. Gardner's integrative versus instrumental motivation. Dörnyei's three parts: ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, L2 learning experience.

sections.title: Intelligence, learner differences and learning styles

blocks.x: Learners differ in abilities, interests and preferences. These theories help teachers vary their teaching, but some popular ideas are not well supported by research, so it matters to know which.
Major ideas

head: Theory
Key figure
Core idea
Evidence and classroom use
rows: A general factor underlies performance on many different mental tests.
A strong predictor of school achievement, but it does not describe everything a learner can do.
Fluid intelligence is reasoning with new problems; crystallized intelligence is learned knowledge and skills.
Knowledge keeps growing, so teach knowledge as well as reasoning.
Intelligence is several relatively independent abilities: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal. Naturalistic was added later.
A useful reminder to vary tasks and ways of representing ideas. Research does not support treating them as fixed “types” of students.
Include analysis tasks, creating or inventing tasks, and real-life application tasks.
The ability to perceive, use, understand and manage emotions in oneself and others.
Teach emotion vocabulary, empathy and conflict resolution as part of social-emotional learning.
Learning styles (VARK, Kolb, Honey and Mumford)
People prefer to receive information in particular ways, for example visual, auditory, read/write or kinesthetic (VARK).

Preferences exist, but studies have not shown that teaching to a learner's “style” improves learning (Pashler and colleagues, 2008). Better: use several modes for everyone and choose the mode that suits the content.

blocks.x: Avoid labelling learners (“she is a kinesthetic learner”). Labels can limit expectations and choices.
In the classroom

items: Present key ideas in more than one form: words, picture, example, action.
Let learners choose how to show learning (write, draw, present) while still assessing the same objective.
Form groups that mix strengths.
Teach social-emotional skills directly, for example how to disagree politely or how to calm down.
Choose modes by content: show a map for geography and let learners speak for pronunciation.

blocks.x: Gardner: multiple intelligences (seven at first, eight with naturalistic). Sternberg: three. Spearman: g. “Learning styles” is a popular idea without strong evidence for matching teaching to style.

sections.title: Human development: Erikson, Kohlberg and Bronfenbrenner

blocks.x: Development theories describe how children and teenagers change in personality, moral reasoning and context. Knowing typical patterns helps teachers choose age-appropriate tasks and expectations. Piaget's cognitive stages are in the Constructivism section.
Erikson's psychosocial stages

Industry vs inferiority: learners need chances to complete tasks successfully and be recognized; repeated failure can lead to feeling inferior. Identity vs role confusion: adolescents explore who they are, so offer choices, responsibilities and discussion of values.
Kohlberg's stages of moral development

head: Level
Stage
Reasoning
rows: Right means what benefits me or is a fair exchange.
Right means being a good person in the eyes of others.
Right means doing one's duty and following rules.
Rules serve the common good and can be changed.
Right is based on justice, rights and conscience.

blocks.x: Kohlberg used moral dilemmas such as the Heinz dilemma and looked at the reasons given, not the decision itself. Carol Gilligan criticized the theory for emphasizing justice over an ethic of care, and cultural bias is also a common criticism.
Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory

head: System
Meaning
Example
rows: Immediate settings the child takes part in
Settings that affect the child indirectly
A parent's workplace; school board decisions
Moving school, a family change, a historical period

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Moral and Civics: use dilemmas and ask “why?” to reveal learners' reasoning, then invite reasoning one stage higher through discussion.
Involve families in learning (the mesosystem): short notes, meetings, home activities.
Give age-appropriate responsibility and chances to finish tasks successfully.
For teenagers, offer real choices, roles and discussion of values.

blocks.x: Stage theories describe typical patterns, not every learner, and cultures differ a great deal.
Piaget is cognitive, Erikson is psychosocial, Kohlberg is moral, and Bronfenbrenner is ecological (context). Kohlberg has three levels and six stages.

Classroom management theories offer ways to prevent misbehavior, build routines and respond fairly. Most well-run classrooms rely mainly on prevention: clear routines, engaging lessons and positive relationships.
Major models

head: Model
Key figure
Core idea
Typical strategies
rows: Prevent problems through good lesson management.
Withitness (aware of everything), overlapping (handle two things at once), smoothness and momentum, group alerting, accountability, and the ripple effect.
The teacher has a right to teach; use clear rules and a consistent set of consequences.
Posted rules, warnings, graded consequences, positive recognition. Criticized as teacher-controlled.
Behavior is chosen to meet five needs: survival, love and belonging, power, freedom and fun.
Meaningful work, class meetings, helping learners take responsibility.
Misbehavior comes from four mistaken goals: attention, power, revenge, avoidance of failure (inadequacy).
Identify the goal, encourage, use logical consequences, hold class meetings.
Use body language, proximity and efficient help to keep learners on task.
Move around, set limits calmly, use group incentives such as preferred activity time.
The teacher's words shape the climate: address the situation, not the learner's character.
“I see papers on the floor” rather than “You are messy”.
B. F. Skinner and applied behavior analysis
Three tiers of support: universal (all learners), targeted (some) and intensive (few). Teach and reinforce expectations.
A few positive rules, specific praise, decisions based on data.
Repair harm and relationships instead of only punishing.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Teach routines in the first weeks (entering, group work, asking for help, finishing early) and practise them.
State three to five rules in positive terms (“Listen when others speak”).
Respond in steps: non-verbal signal (proximity, eye contact, pause), then a quiet private word, and use consequences last, consistently.
Keep lessons moving: have materials ready, give clear instructions, check that learners understood them.
Praise specific behavior and keep far more positive than corrective comments.
After a conflict, repair the relationship.

blocks.x: Group work: the teacher assigns roles (reader, recorder, timekeeper, speaker), displays a timer and a “what to do when finished” task. There are fewer off-task problems because routines and accountability are clear (Kounin).
Kounin: prevention (withitness, overlapping, momentum). Canter: assertive discipline. Dreikurs: four mistaken goals. Glasser: choice theory and five needs.

sections.title: Differentiation, Universal Design for Learning and inclusion

blocks.x: Learners in any class differ in readiness, interests and needs. Differentiation adjusts teaching for those differences, and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) designs the lesson from the start to reduce barriers for everyone.
Differentiated instruction (Carol Ann Tomlinson)

head: Teacher can differentiate…
Examples
rows: Content (what is learned, how learners access it)
Texts at different levels, mini-lessons, audio versions, glossaries
Process (how learners make sense of ideas)
Tiered activities, flexible groups, learning stations, choice boards
Written, spoken, visual or practical outputs judged by the same criteria
Seating, quiet areas, routines, tools available

blocks.x: Differentiation responds to three learner factors: readiness (what the learner can already do), interest, and learning profile (how the learner works best). Pre-assessment and ongoing formative assessment show what to adjust.
Universal Design for Learning (CAST)

head: Principle
Question
Examples
rows: Text with audio and images, captions, glossaries, varied examples
Multiple means of action and expression
Oral or written answers, drawing, models, technology, flexible time

blocks.x: Tiers of support (MTSS and Response to Intervention)

items: Tier 1: high-quality teaching for all learners.
Tier 2: targeted small-group support for those who need more.
Tier 3: intensive, individual support.

blocks.x: Key terms

items: Accommodation: a change in how a learner accesses or shows learning without lowering expectations (extra time, larger print).
Modification: a change in what the learner is expected to learn.
Scaffolding: temporary support that is withdrawn as skill grows.
Inclusive education: all learners learn together, with the support they need.
Individualized education plan (IEP): a written plan of goals and support for a learner with identified needs.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Pre-assess with a quick quiz or KWL chart to find readiness.
Keep the same learning objective for all learners and vary the support, the route and the way of showing learning.
Offer tiered tasks on the same topic at different challenge levels, with a choice menu.
Use flexible groups that change by task, not fixed ability groups.
Provide visuals, word banks and sentence frames, and extension tasks for fast finishers.

blocks.x: English reading: all learners read the same short text. One group receives a glossary and pre-taught words, one answers questions at three levels, and one writes an alternative ending. Groups change in the next task.
The “Differentiation and student support” section of the Planner records the support for learners who need help and the extension for advanced learners.

Differentiation: the teacher adjusts content, process, product and environment. UDL: design the lesson up front to reduce barriers for everyone. Accommodation keeps the expectation; modification changes it.

sections.title: Teaching strategies: cooperative learning, Rosenshine's principles and questioning

blocks.x: Teaching strategies are the “how” of a lesson. The strategies below are widely used and well studied. None works for every goal, so choose by objective and learners.
Cooperative learning
Johnson and Johnson identify five elements that make group work cooperative rather than just seated together.

items: Positive interdependence: group members need each other to succeed.
Individual accountability: each member is responsible for their own learning.
Promotive (face-to-face) interaction: members help and encourage each other.
Social skills: listening, taking turns, disagreeing politely.
Group processing: the group reflects on how well it worked.

head: Structure
How it works
rows: Think alone, discuss with a partner, share with the class.
Groups discuss; the teacher calls a number and that member answers for the group.
Each member becomes an expert on one part, then teaches the others in a new group.
Learners study in teams, take quizzes alone, and team scores come from members' improvement.

blocks.x: Rosenshine's principles of instruction (2012)

items: Begin each lesson with a short review of previous learning.
Present new material in small steps, with practice after each step.
Ask a large number of questions and check the responses of all learners.
Provide models and worked examples.
Guide learner practice.
Check for understanding.
Obtain a high success rate.
Provide scaffolds for difficult tasks.
Require and monitor independent practice.
Engage learners in weekly and monthly review.

blocks.x: Gradual release of responsibility
I do (the teacher models), we do (guided practice), you do together (pairs or groups), you do alone. Support is reduced as learners gain skill.
Questioning

items: Wait time (Mary Budd Rowe, 1974): pausing about three seconds after a question and after an answer gives longer answers and more learners taking part.
Mix closed questions (check facts) and open questions (explore reasoning).
Socratic questioning probes clarity, assumptions, evidence, other viewpoints, consequences and the question itself (Paul and Elder).
Get responses from everyone with mini-whiteboards, cold-calling or response cards instead of only volunteers.

blocks.x: Inquiry and project-based learning

items: Inquiry cycle: question, investigate, explain, share and reflect.
Project-based learning: a driving question, an extended project, a product shared with an audience, feedback and revision.
The teacher plans roles, checkpoints and a rubric; learners need guidance, especially at first.

blocks.x: Jigsaw in History: five expert groups each study one cause of an event, then regroup so that every new group has an expert on each cause and teaches the others. The lesson ends with an individual quiz.
Johnson and Johnson: five elements. Rowe: wait time of three seconds. Rosenshine: ten principles. Jigsaw: Aronson, 1971.
Metacognition means “thinking about thinking”: knowing how you learn and controlling your own learning. Self-regulated learners plan, monitor and evaluate their work, and they usually achieve more.
Key ideas

head: Idea
Key figure
Meaning
Example
rows: Knowledge about the person (how I learn), the task (what it demands) and strategies (what works).
“Essays take me longer than short answers, and I remember better when I draw.”
Planning, monitoring and evaluating one's learning.
Plan time, check understanding while reading, review mistakes.
Feelings and judgments during learning, such as feeling confused or feeling sure.
Forethought (goals, strategy planning, motivation beliefs), performance (self-control, self-observation), self-reflection (self-judgment, reaction). The cycle repeats.
Goal sheet, then working, then a reflection.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Think aloud so that learners hear the thinking behind a solution.
Use KWL charts (Ogle, 1986): what I Know, what I Want to know, what I Learned.
Teach self-questioning: What is my goal? Which strategy will I use? Did it work?
Use exit tickets: “What was clear? What is still confusing?”
After tests, use error analysis or exam wrappers to sort mistakes and plan actions.
Use checklists and rubrics for self-assessment.
Teach reciprocal teaching for reading (Palincsar and Brown, 1984): predict, question, clarify, summarize.

blocks.x: After a maths test, learners sort each error as careless, concept or method, write one action for each, and compare plans with a partner.
Reviews such as the Education Endowment Foundation's Teaching and Learning Toolkit rate metacognition and self-regulation as high impact for low cost.
Metacognition has two parts: knowledge and regulation. Flavell introduced the term (1979). Zimmerman's cycle has three phases: forethought, performance, self-reflection.

Assessment frameworks help teachers decide what to check, when and how to respond. The main shift in recent decades is from assessment only at the end toward using assessment during learning to guide teaching.
Key ideas

head: Idea
Key figure(s)
Core idea
Classroom use
rows: Formative assessment is used during learning to adjust teaching; summative assessment judges achievement at the end.
Check understanding in every lesson with hinge questions, mini-whiteboards and exit tickets.
Assessment for, as and of learning
For: the teacher uses evidence to guide teaching. As: learners monitor their own learning. Of: reports achievement.
Plan all three across a unit.
Criterion-referenced compares performance with a standard; norm-referenced compares learners with each other.
Use criteria so learners know what success looks like.
A scoring guide listing criteria and levels of performance, either analytic (by criterion) or holistic (overall).
Share the rubric before the task; build it with learners.

Three questions: Where am I going? How am I going? Where to next? Feedback works at four levels: task, process, self-regulation and self. Praise aimed at the person (“you're clever”) is the least helpful.
Comment on the process and strategy, and leave time for learners to act on the feedback.

blocks.x: Wiliam's five formative assessment strategies

items: Clarify, share and understand learning intentions and success criteria.
Engineer effective discussions, tasks and questions that elicit evidence of learning.
Provide feedback that moves learners forward.
Activate learners as learning resources for one another.
Activate learners as owners of their own learning.

blocks.x: In the classroom

items: Share success criteria at the start of the lesson.
Use diagnostic questions whose wrong answers reveal particular misconceptions.
Give comments before, or instead of, marks, because grades can overshadow comments.
Build time into the lesson for learners to respond to feedback.
Use peer and self-assessment with a rubric.
Use the results to plan the next lesson, not only to record scores.

blocks.x: The “Assessment and checking understanding” section of the Planner records the assessment method, the evidence that learners achieved the objectives, and the common errors to watch for.
Formative means assessment for learning, summative means assessment of learning. Hattie and Timperley's three questions are often summarized as feed up, feed back and feed forward.
Philosophies of education are beliefs about the purpose of school, what should be taught and how teachers should teach. They explain why teachers, schools and policies differ.
Major philosophies

head: Philosophy
Key figures
Purpose of education
Curriculum and method
Teacher's role
rows: Develop the mind through enduring truths and great ideas.
Great books and classical subjects; Socratic seminar; the same core for all.
Authority who leads discussion of great ideas.
Pass on the essential knowledge and skills of the culture.
Core subjects (reading, writing, maths, science, history); discipline and testing.
Develop the whole child and prepare for democratic life.
Learner interests, problem solving, projects, learning by doing.
Use schools to build a better, fairer society.
Social issues, community projects, critical thinking.
Help each person find meaning and take responsibility for choices.
Choice of topics; arts and humanities; self-expression.
Helps learners discover themselves through dialogue.
Free learners from oppression by developing critical awareness.
Problem-posing education and dialogue about real-life issues.
Co-learner who enters dialogue with learners.
Prepared environment, hands-on materials, mixed ages, long uninterrupted work periods.

blocks.x: The “banking” concept treats learners as empty accounts into which the teacher deposits knowledge. Problem-posing education has teachers and learners investigate real problems together.

Perennialism and essentialism are usually described as teacher-centered. Progressivism, existentialism, critical pedagogy and humanism are student-centered. Most teachers blend ideas, for example a core of essential knowledge taught through progressive projects.
In the classroom

items: Ask yourself why you teach a topic and how learners learn it best. Your answers show your working philosophy.
Notice mismatches, for example valuing creativity but only assessing recall.
Use these labels to justify choices in exam essays and teacher interviews.

blocks.x: Perennialism and essentialism are teacher-centered. Progressivism is linked to Dewey. Reconstructionism aims at social change. Freire is linked to critical pedagogy and the banking versus problem-posing contrast.
